flashcards.back: Human language is generative and shared to communicate meaning; LLM output is combinatorial with no communicative intention.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: What is a performative speech act?
flashcards.back: An utterance that performs an action and changes reality (e.g., 'I now pronounce you married'), given proper authority, sincerity, and audience uptake.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: J. L. Austin ('How to Do Things With Words') and Judith Butler (who extended it to gender/identity).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Offense = harm to the hearers/viewers (impact); derogation = the utterer's disparaging attitude. An expression can be one, both, or neither.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Vulgarity = taboo bodily reference (shit, ass); expletive = outburst term (damn). Some words are both.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: What makes something a slur (vs. a particularistic insult)?
flashcards.back: A slur denigrates a whole marginalized GROUP and depends on a power imbalance; a particularistic insult condemns one person for specific behavior.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Their emotional power comes from a power differential and the invocation of historical violence — even mentioning some can harm.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Using a word refers to a thing; mentioning a word treats the word itself as a linguistic object (shown in italics).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: How does a matched-guise study work?
flashcards.back: Hold the STIMULUS constant, vary the GUISE; any rating difference is due to the guise (the label), revealing hidden attitudes.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: In the résumé study, what were stimulus and guise?
flashcards.back: Stimulus = the (constant) résumé; guise = the name at the top (English- vs. non-English-sounding).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Replacing/mispronouncing a name to make it 'sound more English/white,' erasing identity (Bucholtz).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Unspecified singular 'they' is ~600 years old; the NEW change is SPECIFIC singular 'they' for a known person.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Can anyone stop language from changing?
flashcards.back: No. Language change is inevitable; prescriptive complaints don't stop it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: The killing of a language through policy (e.g., residential schools forbidding Indigenous languages).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Why do L2 users have accents?
flashcards.back: Their L2 mental grammar is shaped by their L1's phonology; accent 'reduction' is hard after childhood — but comprehension adapts more easily.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Modality of spoken vs. signed languages?
flashcards.back: Spoken = vocal-auditory; signed = manual-visual.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Three parts of a full consonant description (and order)?
flashcards.back: Phonation – Place – Manner (e.g., voiced bilabial nasal stop).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Active = the moving/lower articulator; passive = the target/upper articulator.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Name the 4 core manners (this book) + affricate.
flashcards.back: Stop, fricative, approximant, (+ affricate = plosive with fricated release).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Oral vs. nasal stop — what differs?
flashcards.back: Velum position: raised = oral stop; lowered = nasal stop (air through the nose).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Obstruents = oral stops, fricatives, affricates (big obstruction); sonorants = nasals, approximants, taps, trills (free airflow).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Voiced = vocal folds vibrate (buzz [z]); voiceless = no vibration (bus [s]).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Three main dimensions of vowel quality?
flashcards.back: Height (vertical tongue), backness (horizontal tongue), rounding (lip shape).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Central = intermediate BACKNESS; mid = intermediate HEIGHT.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Tense = advanced tongue root (beat); lax = retracted tongue root (bit).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: What is the IPA and why like the periodic table?
flashcards.back: A one-symbol-per-phone transcription system; its organizing principles matter more than rote symbol memorization.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Handshape, orientation, location, movement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Path vs. local movement in signs?
flashcards.back: Path = elbow/shoulder (moves through space); local = wrist/radioulnar/knuckles.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Two signs differing in exactly one parameter (e.g., SORRY vs. PLEASE = handshape only).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Onset (optional) + nucleus (required, usually a vowel) + coda (optional).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Closed = has a coda; open = no coda; onsetless = no onset.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Sonority rises through the onset, peaks at the nucleus, falls through the coda.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Primary = upper tick [ˈ]; secondary = lower tick [ˌ]; before the syllable's onset.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Tone = pitch on syllables/words changing meaning; intonation = pitch over phrases/sentences for functions (question vs. statement).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.back: Phoneme = abstract category /x/; allophones = its physical realizations [ ] in specific environments.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: / / = phonemic (UR); [ ] = phonetic (SR/phones); < > = spelling/orthography.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: What proves two phones are contrastive (different phonemes)?
flashcards.back: One minimal pair — same context, one phone differs, different meaning.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: The two phones never share an environment. Same phoneme if phonetically similar; different phonemes if not (e.g., [h]/[ŋ]).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Two allophones of English /t/ and their environments?
flashcards.back: [ɾ] before an unstressed vowel (atom); [tʰ] before a stressed vowel (atomic).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: A set of phones sharing phonetic properties AND phonological behaviour; must include ALL such phones in the language.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Three parts of a phonological rule?
flashcards.back: Target (A) → change (B) / environment (C _ D).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: UR = underlying/phonemic /x/ (input); SR = surface/phonetic [x] (output). Rules derive SR from UR.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: Absent any rule, a phoneme surfaces as its default allophone ('elsewhere' case) — so we don't write that statement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: Given equal data coverage, choose the analysis with fewer rules/statements.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: A phoneme changes to match a property in its environment (e.g., sonorants devoice after a voiceless obstruent).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: If no minimal pair exists, what tools help?
flashcards.back: Near-minimal pairs (need several) and nonce-word judgments.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Do signed languages have productive phonological rules?
flashcards.back: Not the fully productive kind; they have sign-specific processes (weak hand freeze/drop, lowering) affecting individual signs.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: In a two-handed sign where both hands move, both must share handshape and movement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.back: The smallest systematic pairing of form and meaning/grammatical function (e.g., cat, -s).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: The smallest separable unit — can stand alone and reorder in a sentence (not the spelling/spaces definition).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: Root = indivisible core; base = whatever an affix attaches to (can be complex); affix = bound morpheme needing a base.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: Prefix (before), suffix (after), circumfix (around), infix (inside), simultaneous (at the same time).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: Free = can stand alone (cat); bound = must attach (all affixes + bound roots like -whelmed). Only roots can be free.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: Internal change (mouse→mice), suppletion (go→went), reduplication (salad-salad).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: Allomorphs = the variant forms of one morpheme; allomorphy = the phenomenon of a morpheme having them.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: Phonological = chosen by nearby sounds (a/an); lexical = chosen by the specific root, memorized (ox→oxen).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: Derivation can change meaning/category; inflection expresses grammatical info and NEVER changes category.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: How are lexical categories defined in linguistics?
flashcards.back: By distribution (grammatical contexts a word appears in), not by meaning ('action word').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: A word built from two or more roots (blackboard); in English, stressed on the first member.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Isolating vs. synthetic; agglutinative vs. fusional?
flashcards.back: Isolating = few morphemes/word (Mandarin); synthetic = many. Agglutinative = separable one-meaning affixes; fusional = one affix, many meanings.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: A morpheme with no overt form (e.g., plural of sheep).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.back: One string with two possible structures → two meanings (e.g., unlockable).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: What are the two most common basic word orders?
flashcards.back: SOV (most common, ~41%) and SVO (~35%, incl. English). All six orders are attested.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: A clause = subject + predicate; a sentence = a clause that stands alone. Clauses can be embedded inside others.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: 1 argument (subject) / 2 (subject+object) / 3 (subject + two objects).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Simple = one clause; compound = clauses joined by and/or/but; complex = has an embedded clause (recursion).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: A group of words acting as a single structural unit, identified by constituency tests.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Substitution (pro-form), movement, it-cleft, stand-alone (fragment) answer, and (weakly) coordination.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Head = the obligatory central word; complement = a phrase the head selects; specifier = phrase at the phrase's top edge (e.g., subject = specifier of TP).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Lexical (N, V, Adj, Adv) name things/events; functional (D, T/Aux, C, pronouns, conjunctions) are grammatical glue.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Introduces an embedded clause (that, if, whether); it's the head C of a CP.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Agent (does on purpose), experiencer (mental state), theme/patient (thing affected), instrument (tool used).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Every phrase XP is a projection of a head X via an intermediate X' (bar level), with specifier, complement, and adjunct positions.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Why is a sentence a TP?
flashcards.back: Because it's always headed by tense (an auxiliary, tense on the verb, or nonfinite 'to'); subject = specifier of TP, VP = complement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: A complementizer phrase — embedded clauses are CPs, and it's the landing site for T-to-C and wh-movement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: How are English yes-no questions formed (in X-bar terms)?
flashcards.back: Subject-Auxiliary Inversion = T-to-C head movement (the auxiliary moves from T up to C).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: With a wh-word via wh-movement — the wh-phrase moves to the front (specifier of CP).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: A modifier attached at an extra bar level — neither specifier nor complement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Agent acts on purpose (The pirate sank it); experiencer undergoes a mental state (Pirates frighten me).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: What does the passive do to argument structure?
flashcards.back: It rearranges arguments (the theme becomes subject; the agent is demoted/optional), changing argument structure without changing the event's roles.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.back: Linguistic = meaning encoded by words/sentences (sense of 'swill'); non-linguistic = 'clouds mean rain', a gift 'means' I'm sorry.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: Sense = the concept stored in your head; denotation = what the expression points to in the world (⟦pencil⟧ = the set of all pencils).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: A complex meaning depends on the meanings of the parts AND how they're combined — not just which words, but the structure.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: Negate it: negating an entailment (while keeping the original) is a contradiction; an implicature is cancellable (no contradiction).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: A special entailment the sentence takes for granted as already true (e.g., 'The professor petted a cat again' presupposes a previous petting).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Why isn't meaning just necessary & sufficient conditions?
flashcards.back: The 'cup or bowl' experiments show category boundaries are fuzzy and depend on world knowledge — prototypes, not strict definitions.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: Count = countable, pluralizes, takes 'many' (cats); mass = uncountable substance, takes 'much' (water).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: Individual-level = stable property (is tall); stage-level = temporary state (is available / being restless now).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: 'The denotation of x' — what the expression x points to; for a one-place predicate, the set of things it's true of.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: What is a negative polarity item (NPI)?
flashcards.back: A word like 'any/ever' licensed only in negative/downward-entailing contexts (*'I saw anyone' vs. 'I didn't see anyone').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: No — idioms ('let the cat out of the bag') are non-compositional and stored whole.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Is a dictionary the authority on meaning?
flashcards.back: No — dictionaries lag usage and don't list all senses; meaning lives in speakers' minds, not the OED.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.back: At-issue = literal surface meaning (targeted by 'it is not the case that…'); non-at-issue = implicatures/presuppositions (not targeted).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: An inference beyond the literal meaning, drawn by assuming the speaker is being cooperative; it's cancellable.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: In conversation, cooperate toward the accepted purpose of the talk — the basis for computing implicatures.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: Quality (be truthful), Quantity (be appropriately informative), Relation (be relevant), Manner (be clear/brief/orderly).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: Flouting = blatantly breaking a maxim to trigger an implicature (sarcasm); violating = quietly breaking it (lying), no implicature intended.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: What you DO with an utterance — assert, ask, order — the act performed in saying it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: Assertion = put a proposition forward as true; question = invite the addressee to supply information.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: An act performed by uttering (asserting, questioning, promising, pronouncing); works across modalities.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: Because you can deny/suspend it without contradiction — unlike an entailment.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: The shared situation participants mutually take as established; utterances are interpreted against it and update it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: No — like implicatures, presuppositions are non-at-issue (survive 'it is not the case that…').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: Do all cultures apply the maxims identically?
flashcards.back: No — e.g., the Maxim of Quality is parameterized differently across communities (Mopan/Mopan Maya study).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.back: A community reclaiming active use of its heritage language, especially after colonial suppression.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.back: Reclamation = a community reclaiming its language; revitalization = restoring its vitality by growing speakers and everyday use.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Dr. Kanatawakhon-Maracle's core point about survival?
flashcards.back: For a language to survive it must be widely SPOKEN — used in daily life, not just supported in principle.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.back: Language carries cultural knowledge; e.g., Mohawk 'nyaweh' means far more than English 'thank you.'
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.back: A mixed language of the Métis combining Algonquian (Cree/Ojibwe) and French elements.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.back: A distinct, historically multilingual Indigenous people associated with Michif, spread across the Prairies and into North Dakota.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.back: A setting where learners are surrounded by and use the target language (e.g., Six Nations Mohawk immersion).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: What drove Indigenous-language endangerment in Canada?
flashcards.back: The legacy of colonialism, including residential schools, which suppressed the languages and made speaking them feel shameful.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Name three languages featured in this chapter.
flashcards.back: Kanien'kéha (Mohawk), Michif, Hul'q'umi'num' (plus Nishnaabemwin).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Role of fluent Elders in reclamation?
flashcards.back: They are key mentors — sources of the language and the stories/knowledge carried in it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.back: A place where speakers have two+ ways of saying the same thing in the same environment (e.g., -ing: walking/walkin').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: The variable is the choice point (-ing); the variants are the alternatives ([ɪŋ] vs. [ɪn]).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: Cross-linguistic = between different languages; sociolinguistic = within one language/variety (even one speaker).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: 'Dialect' can carry a loaded 'lesser' connotation; 'variety' is neutral. Everyone speaks a variety; none is 'better.'
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: Idiolect = one individual's variety; vernacular = natural unmonitored speech (how you talk when not being recorded).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: To study natural speech linguists must observe it — but observing makes it less natural.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: Varying speech by situation; the attention-paid-to-speech model links careful speech to more attention.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: Overt = open prestige of the standard variety; covert = hidden in-group prestige of a non-standard form (toughness/solidarity).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: Apparent-time = compare age groups at one time; real-time = compare the community at two actual times.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: Above = conscious, often from higher-prestige speech; below = below awareness, via the vernacular.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: What are the three waves of sociolinguistics?
flashcards.back: 1st: variable × broad social category; 2nd: locally meaningful community facts; 3rd: variation as active identity/style-making.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.back: A categorical alternation fully forced by the linguistic environment (no social choice).

flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: When does vocal babbling begin, and what about deaf babies?
flashcards.back: ~0;6 for both hearing and deaf babies; babies in a signing environment also babble on the hands (manual babbling).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.back: Repeated CV syllables like [bababa]/[dadada].
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.back: Babbling reflects the ambient language (signed or spoken), not just random motor noise.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.back: Overextension = word used too broadly (all bearded men = 'Dada'); underextension = word used too narrowly.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.back: Early multiword speech with mostly content words, omitting function words (like a telegram).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: How does the high-amplitude sucking method work?
flashcards.back: Sucking rate rises to novelty, falls with habituation; a rise again (dishabituation) shows the baby noticed a change.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.back: Infants start sensitive to many contrasts, then tune to their ambient language's contrasts and lose unused ones.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.back: The child has internalized the regular rule and is applying it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: What is the wug test for?
flashcards.back: Showing children apply morphological rules productively to novel words (one wug → two wugs).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.back: Two years, six months (age notation = year;month).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.back: Critical = a hard window for native-like acquisition; sensitive = a softer span of heightened readiness.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: Can children acquire two languages natively at once?
flashcards.back: Yes — simultaneous bilinguals separate the systems and can reach native competence in each.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: How do adult learners differ from children?
flashcards.back: They have mature cognition, an existing language system, and different motivations — so the process differs from child acquisition.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.back: A learner's own evolving, rule-governed system, separate from both L1 and the target L2.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.back: Positive = an existing feature matches the target and helps; negative = a mismatch interferes (source of accent/errors).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.back: Transfer from the phonology of the learner's first language.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.back: Standardized scales (ACTFL, CEFR/Canadian Language Benchmarks) for rating how well someone uses a language.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.back: Declarative = conscious, fact-like (knowing a rule); procedural = automatic skill (fluent real-time use).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: What happens when learning a new modality (M2)?
flashcards.back: Hearing learners of a signed language at first transfer existing iconic gesture before acquiring the linguistic system.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: How does age of acquisition matter?
flashcards.back: Earlier onset generally means more native-like attainment, especially for pronunciation.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.back: Learners usually understand more than they can produce; both grow with proficiency.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.back: No — it's a systematic, rule-governed system of its own, a normal stage of learning.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.back: Psycholinguistics studies the mental processes of language (via behaviour, e.g., reaction times); neurolinguistics studies the brain basis (via brain measures like EEG).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: What does 'psychological reality' of phonemes mean?
flashcards.back: That phonemes are actually used by the mind/brain, not just analysts' abstractions — supported by experiments.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.back: Bottom-up = the incoming signal flowing to the brain; top-down = existing knowledge (e.g., of words) shaping perception.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: Give an example of a top-down effect.
flashcards.back: Your knowledge of real words biases how you perceive an ambiguous sound on a [d]-[t] continuum toward a real word.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.back: Your native language shapes how your brain processes input (e.g., which contrasts it responds to).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: What do EEG studies suggest about phonological contrasts?
flashcards.back: The brain registers them very early in processing, before higher-level language areas engage.

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 13
notes.body: ★ PSYCHOLINGUISTICS = mental processes of production/comprehension (behavioural methods, e.g., reaction times). NEUROLINGUISTICS = brain basis (e.g., EEG). ★ Evidence supports the PSYCHOLOGICAL REALITY of phonemes — they're used by the mind/brain, not just analysts' abstractions. ★ Processing is LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC (native language shapes it). ★ Perception = BOTTOM-UP (signal→brain) + TOP-DOWN (word knowledge shapes perception, e.g., [d]-[t] continuum). ★ Brain registers phonological contrasts EARLY. [Chapter marked in progress in source.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

notes.title: 13.4 Top-down effects of word knowledge
notes.body: Perception combines bottom-up information (the incoming signal flowing to the brain) with top-down influences (existing knowledge shaping perception). A speaker's knowledge of the words of their language affects the sounds they hear — e.g., on a [d]-to-[t] continuum, word knowledge biases perception toward real words. This top-down effect operates early, showing language knowledge shapes processing from an early stage.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

notes.title: 13.3 Language-specific processing
notes.body: Processing is shaped by the specific language a person knows: a speaker's native language influences how they process incoming linguistic input, including which phonological contrasts their brain responds to. This shows that linguistic knowledge, not just the raw signal, drives perception.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

notes.title: 13.1-13.2 The mind makes language; phonemes are real
notes.body: Language is produced and understood by mental processes. A recurring question is whether the abstract units of linguistic theory have psychological reality. Psycho- and neurolinguistic experiments provide evidence that phonemes are real to the mind/brain — for instance, brain responses distinguish phonological contrasts, supporting phonology as something the mind and brain actually use.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

notes.title: Chapter 13 — Overview
notes.body: Psycholinguistics and neurolinguistics ask how the mind and brain actually make language. Psycholinguistics uses behavioural experiments (e.g., reaction times) to evaluate theories of production and comprehension; neurolinguistics uses brain measures (e.g., EEG). This short chapter focuses on evidence that abstract units like phonemes are psychologically real. [The chapter is marked in progress in the source.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 12
notes.body: ★ SLA = learning a language after childhood (framed broadly, incl. reclamation). Adults ≠ children: mature cognition, existing L1, different motivations. ★ INTERLANGUAGE (Selinker) = the learner's own rule-governed system between L1 and L2 — not 'broken' language. ★ TRANSFER: POSITIVE (shared feature helps, e.g., an already-known contrast) vs. NEGATIVE (mismatch interferes → accent/errors). L2 ACCENT comes from L1 phonology. ★ PROFICIENCY measured by BENCHMARKS (ACTFL, CEFR/Canadian Language Benchmarks). ★ DECLARATIVE (conscious rule-knowledge) vs. PROCEDURAL (automatic skill). ★ NEW-MODALITY (M2) learners transfer iconic gesture before the signed system. ★ Earlier AGE OF ACQUISITION → more native-like attainment (esp. pronunciation).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

notes.title: 12.5-12.7 New modality; phonetics & phonemes
notes.body: Learning a language in a new modality — e.g., a hearing person learning a signed language (an M2 learner) — shows learners transferring existing iconic, non-linguistic gesture before acquiring the signed system. In learning pronunciation, positive transfer is predicted when the new language has a phoneme contrast the learner already has, and negative transfer where contrasts differ; this shapes the persistent 'accent' of the interlanguage stage.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

notes.title: 12.4 Cognitive processes & interlanguage
notes.body: Learners build an interlanguage (Selinker 1972): their own evolving, rule-governed system between the L1 and the target language. Transfer from existing languages can be positive (a shared feature helps — e.g., an already-known phoneme contrast) or negative (a mismatch interferes, a major source of L2 accent). Two memory systems are relevant: declarative knowledge (conscious, fact-like — knowing a rule) and procedural knowledge (automatic skill — fluent real-time use); later learning often leans more on declarative knowledge.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

notes.title: 12.3 Gaining proficiency
notes.body: Gaining proficiency in a later language means moving, in both comprehension and production, from limited ability toward more native-like use. Proficiency is measured with standardized benchmarks — e.g., ACTFL Proficiency Guidelines (five levels) or the CEFR/Canadian Language Benchmarks — which are used by programs including Indigenous-language reclamation schools (e.g., Onkwawenna Kentyohkwa).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

notes.title: 12.1-12.2 Adults are not children; motivations
notes.body: Adult learners are not just older children: they bring mature cognition, an already-established first language, and distinct motivations. Reasons for learning a later language vary widely (work, migration, connection, and — importantly in this text — language reclamation), and these motivations shape how and how well people learn.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

notes.title: Chapter 12 — Overview
notes.body: This chapter covers learning a language later in life — often called Second Language Acquisition (SLA), framed broadly to include reclamation and any post-childhood learning. It contrasts adult and child learners, motivations for learning, how proficiency is gained and measured, cognitive processes, and the special case of learning a new modality (a signed language).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 11
notes.body: ★ AGE notation year;month (2;6 = 2 yrs 6 mo). ★ HIGH-AMPLITUDE SUCKING: novelty↑, habituation↓, DISHABITUATION↑ = infant detected a change. ★ PERCEPTUAL NARROWING: broad→ambient-language contrasts. ★ BABBLING ~0;6 (hearing & deaf); CANONICAL = [bababa]; MANUAL babbling on the hands = babbling reflects ambient language. ★ FIRST WORDS ~0;12 (earlier in sign). OVEREXTENSION (too broad, 'Dada' for all beards) vs. UNDEREXTENSION (too narrow). ★ TELEGRAPHIC speech = content words, function words dropped. ★ OVERREGULARIZATION ('goed') = rule learned; WUG TEST = productive morphology. ★ CRITICAL vs. SENSITIVE period. ★ Simultaneous BILINGUAL children reach native competence in each language.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

notes.title: 11.9-11.10 Bilingualism & milestones
notes.body: Children can grow up bilingual (or multilingual): simultaneous bilinguals separate their languages and can reach native competence in each; apparent 'mixing' is normal and rule-governed. The chapter maps typical milestones (babbling → first words → two-word/telegraphic → complex sentences) across the early years, noting comparable stages in signed-language acquisition.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

notes.title: 11.7-11.8 Early syntax
notes.body: Early multiword speech is telegraphic — mostly content words, omitting obligatory function words like determiners. Children's errors are rule-governed: overregularization ('goed', 'foots') shows they've learned regular patterns, and non-adult sentences ('My cereal is very milk', 'The want babies some milk') reveal an emerging grammar rather than random noise. The wug test shows productive rule use with novel words.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

notes.title: 11.5-11.6 Environment, methods & word learning
notes.body: Studying acquisition requires sampling children's speech (e.g., recording fixed or random one-hour windows) — each method trades off naturalness and coverage. In word learning, children exploit morphosyntactic cues: adjective vs. noun frames ('the feppy one' → the odd-patterned object; 'the fep' → the novel object) and mass/count syntax ('some corvel' vs. 'a corvel') guide what a new word refers to.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

notes.title: 11.4 Early production: babbling & first words
notes.body: Vocal babbling begins ~0;6 in both hearing and deaf babies; canonical babbling is repeated CV syllables ([bababa]). Deaf babies' vocal babbling drops off (no vocal input to shape it), while babies in signing environments babble on the hands (manual babbling) — showing babbling reflects the ambient language. First words appear ~0;12 (often earlier, ~0;8-0;9, in sign) and are similar across children. Word meanings are often overextended (bearded men all 'Dada'; a motorcycle called by the car-word) or underextended.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

notes.title: 11.1-11.3 Powerful learners, timing & phonemic contrast
notes.body: Infants are powerful language learners shaped by their environment (a child adopted at birth acquires the adoptive family's language). Methods like high-amplitude sucking exploit habituation/dishabituation: sucking rate rises to novelty, falls with habituation, and rises again when the baby detects a change. Newborns already track prosodic rhythm from the womb. Through perceptual narrowing, infants tune from broad sensitivity to the phonemic contrasts of their ambient language — so a contrast present in the input is likely to be acquired, while an unused one fades.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

notes.title: Chapter 11 — Overview
notes.body: Children acquire language rapidly and systematically. This chapter surveys the milestones and the methods used to study pre-verbal infants, from perception (high-amplitude sucking) to production (babbling, first words, telegraphic speech), plus word learning, early syntax, and bilingual acquisition. Ages use the notation year;month (e.g., 2;6).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 10
notes.body: ★ SOCIOLINGUISTIC variation = within one language/variety (vs. CROSS-LINGUISTIC = between languages). ★ LINGUISTIC VARIABLE = two+ ways to say the same thing in the same environment; VARIANTS = the alternatives (-ing: [ɪŋ]/[ɪn]). NOT variables: synonyms, categorical (environment-forced) alternations. ★ Everyone has a DIALECT/VARIETY; none is 'better.' IDIOLECT = one person; VERNACULAR = unmonitored speech. OBSERVER'S PARADOX = observing changes the speech. ★ STYLE-SHIFTING (Labov: attention-paid-to-speech). INDEXICALITY: referential vs. non-referential; ENREGISTERMENT (e.g., 'eh'). ★ Track change in APPARENT time (age groups now) vs. REAL time (two actual times); CHANGE FROM ABOVE (conscious) vs. BELOW (unaware). ★ SOCIOLINGUISTIC CORRELATIONS with class, gender, age, ethnicity, style. OVERT (standard) vs. COVERT (non-standard, solidarity) PRESTIGE. ★ THREE WAVES: (1) broad categories → (2) local community facts → (3) variation as identity/style construction.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

notes.title: 10.10 Three waves of sociolinguistics
notes.body: The field's history is often told as three waves. First wave: correlate variables with broad, predefined social categories (class, sex, age). Second wave: add locally meaningful, community-specific facts about participants (ethnographic detail). Third wave: treat variation as active work — speakers use variants to construct identity and style, not just reflect fixed categories. Each wave builds on, rather than replaces, the previous.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

notes.title: 10.6-10.9 Sociolinguistic correlations
notes.body: A central finding is that linguistic variables correlate systematically with social factors — social class, gender/sex, age, and ethnicity — and with style. Classic cases include Fischer's -ing study (standardized [ɪŋ] vs. [ɪn]) showing both social and stylistic patterning. These correlations are statistical tendencies, read off quantitative graphs, not absolute rules. Prestige matters in two directions: overt prestige for the standardized variety and covert prestige for non-standard forms that index toughness or local solidarity.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

notes.title: 10.5 Variationist methods & concepts
notes.body: Sociolinguists elicit natural speech but face the observer's paradox: observing speech makes it less natural, so eliciting the vernacular (unmonitored speech) is a core challenge (often via the sociolinguistic interview). Variationist methods descend from dialectology, whose dialect maps were biased toward N.O.R.M. participants (non-mobile older rural males). Change can be tracked in apparent time (comparing age groups now) or real time (comparing the community at two actual times), and can be change from above (conscious, higher-prestige) or below (below awareness).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

notes.title: 10.3-10.4 Language changes & conveys social meaning
notes.body: Variation is the seed of language change: e.g., English negation shifted gradually from VERB-NEGATIVE order to 'do not VERB' over time. Beyond referential content, language conveys social meaning through indexicality — referential indexicality points to context, while non-referential indexicality signals social identity or stance. Bundles of features can undergo enregisterment, becoming recognized 'ways of speaking' (e.g., Canadian 'eh'). Speakers also style-shift: Labov's attention-paid-to-speech model links more careful speech to more self-monitoring, though other motivations for shifting exist.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

notes.title: 10.1-10.2 Variationist sociolinguistics & variables
notes.body: Variationist sociolinguistics quantifies variants of linguistic variables to uncover social patterns; it grew out of dialectology. Sociolinguistic variation is variation within one language/variety (even within one person), unlike cross-linguistic variation between languages. A linguistic variable is a point where speakers have two or more ways of expressing the same thing in the same linguistic environment; its alternatives are variants (e.g., the -ing variable: [ɪŋ] walking vs. [ɪn] walkin'). Variables exist in all languages, all modalities, and all domains. Not everything counts: synonyms (different meanings/uses) and categorical alternations (forced by the environment) are not sociolinguistic variables. Everyone speaks a dialect/variety, and no variety is linguistically 'better' (recall Chapter 2).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

notes.title: Chapter 10 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 10 you should be able to: explain the difference between cross-linguistic and sociolinguistic variation; define key sociolinguistics concepts; recognize linguistic variables in data; discuss major findings of variationist sociolinguistics; and interpret basic quantitative sociolinguistic graphs.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 9
notes.body: ★ RECLAMATION = a community reclaiming active use of its language; REVITALIZATION = restoring its vitality (more speakers, everyday use). ★ A language must be actively SPOKEN to survive (Kanatawakhon-Maracle). ★ LANGUAGE + CULTURE are inseparable — words carry cultural meaning (Mohawk 'nyaweh' ≫ 'thank you'). ★ IMMERSION (e.g., Six Nations) builds understanding; the goal is genuine SPEAKERS. ★ MICHIF = a MIXED language of the MÉTIS (Algonquian + French). ★ Featured languages: Kanien'kéha (Mohawk), Michif, Hul'q'umi'num', Nishnaabemwin. ★ Reclamation responds to the LEGACY OF COLONIALISM (residential schools, shame around speaking) and is intergenerational and relationship-based, centring fluent Elders.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

notes.title: 9.8-9.11 Hul'q'umi'num', Nishnaabemwin & resources
notes.body: Further sections describe reclaiming Hul'q'umi'num' (a Coast Salish language) through family- and community-based work — often anchored by a fluent grandmother/Elder and the stories she carries — and learning Nishnaabemwin (an Anishinaabe/Ojibwe variety) in a university/community setting. The chapter closes with resources for teaching and learning these languages. Across all cases, reclamation is intergenerational, relationship-based, and tied to cultural continuity.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

notes.title: 9.7 Reclaiming Michif
notes.body: A contributor and citizen of the Métis Nation Saskatchewan describes working with the languages of the Michif/Métis people. Michif is a mixed language drawing on Algonquian languages (Cree, Ojibwe, Saulteaux) and French. The Métis have long been multilingual, with relatives among Cree, Ojibwe, and settler communities, and a homeland spread widely across the western provinces and into North Dakota — which shapes how reclamation happens across dispersed communities.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

notes.title: 9.4-9.6 Teaching materials & the future (Mohawk)
notes.body: The chapter discusses creating teaching materials, the realities of speaking Mohawk day-to-day, and one contributor's view of the language's future. A recurring theme is moving learners from understanding toward genuine speaking, and building the resources (written and spoken) a living language community needs.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

notes.title: 9.1-9.3 Preserving, learning & culture (Mohawk)
notes.body: Dr. David Kanatawakhon-Maracle (Turtle Clan Mohawk, Western University) argues that for a language to survive it must be widely spoken — verbal support isn't enough if people aren't actually using it. He is both a speaker and literate in Mohawk, a goal for university-level learners since much is written in the language. Many learn Mohawk by growing up among fluent speakers; others learn in school or immersion (e.g., Six Nations), though immersion learners may gain a feel for the language without yet becoming speakers. He deliberately teaches culture with language: words carry cultural weight (e.g., 'nyaweh' is far weightier than English 'thank you'), and knowledge comes from Elders.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

notes.title: Chapter 9 — Overview
notes.body: Chapter 9 centres Indigenous voices on reclaiming their languages. Rather than abstract theory, it presents first-person accounts from language teachers and community members working on Kanien'kéha (Mohawk), Michif, Hul'q'umi'num', and Nishnaabemwin. Common threads: languages must be actively spoken to survive; language and culture are inseparable; and reclamation responds to the harms of colonialism, including residential schools. [Content note: colonial harm, residential schools.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 8
notes.body: ★ AT-ISSUE (literal, surface, truth-conditional) vs. NON-AT-ISSUE (implicatures, presuppositions). Diagnostic: 'it is not the case that…' targets ONLY at-issue meaning. ★ CONVERSATIONAL IMPLICATURE = inference beyond the literal, via assuming cooperation; CANCELLABLE. ★ COOPERATIVE PRINCIPLE (Grice) + four MAXIMS: QUALITY (truthful), QUANTITY (right amount of info), RELATION (relevant), MANNER (clear/brief/orderly). ★ VIOLATING (quietly break, e.g., lying) vs. FLOUTING (blatantly break to trigger an implicature, e.g., sarcasm). ★ ILLOCUTIONARY meaning = what you DO: ASSERTION (put forward as true) vs. QUESTION (request info); these are SPEECH ACTS. ★ CONTEXT = common ground; meaning is DYNAMIC — assertions update the common ground, questions set up answer spaces. ★ Pragmatic norms vary across cultures and minds (neurodiversity).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

notes.title: 8.11-8.14 Context & dynamic meaning
notes.body: A context is the shared situation / common ground — what participants mutually take to be established. Meaning is dynamic: an assertion (if accepted) updates the common ground by adding its content; a question sets up the space of possible answers. Interpreting an utterance both depends on the current context and changes it for what comes next.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

notes.title: 8.9-8.10 Illocutionary meaning & speech acts
notes.body: Illocutionary meaning is what a speaker/signer does in making an utterance — the act performed. Classifying by illocution: an assertion puts a proposition forward as true; a question invites the addressee to supply information; imperatives give orders. These are speech acts (the term applies in all modalities; performatives like 'I now pronounce you married' are one kind). The same literal sentence can perform different acts in context.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

notes.title: 8.7-8.8 Violating vs. flouting
notes.body: A speaker can fail a maxim in two ways. Violating = quietly failing (e.g., lying by breaking Quality) with no intent for the listener to infer extra meaning. Flouting = blatantly, obviously breaking a maxim so the listener, still assuming cooperation, derives an implicature (e.g., heavy sarcasm floats Quality; 'It's a lovely day' during a storm). What counts as satisfying a maxim (e.g., Quality) can also differ across cultures.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

notes.title: 8.4-8.6 Conversational implicature & the Cooperative Principle
notes.body: A conversational implicature is an inference a listener draws beyond the literal meaning by assuming the speaker is cooperating. Grice's Cooperative Principle: contribute as required by the accepted purpose of the talk. It's fleshed out by four maxims — Quality (be truthful), Quantity (be appropriately informative — not too little or too much), Relation (be relevant), and Manner (be clear, brief, orderly). Listeners assume the maxims hold, so apparent breaches trigger inferences (e.g., 'Some students passed' implicates 'not all' via Quantity).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

notes.title: 8.2-8.3 Diversity & the mind
notes.body: What counts as cooperative or 'honest' can vary across communities, and people compute non-at-issue meaning differently (neurodiversity in pragmatics). Pragmatic meaning is real cognitive work, not a fixed literal decoding — so it's important not to treat one community's or one mind's pragmatic norms as the only valid ones.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

notes.title: 8.1 At-issue vs. non-at-issue meaning
notes.body: The at-issue meaning is the main literal 'surface' meaning; other meanings are non-at-issue. Test: sentential negation 'it is not the case that…' targets ONLY the at-issue meaning. So for 'Mounissa will buy the discounted strawberries': at-issue = she'll buy them; non-at-issue implicature = she likes strawberries; non-at-issue presupposition = there are discounted strawberries. Because negation leaves the implicature and presupposition intact, both are non-at-issue. (Some texts call at-issue meaning 'truth-conditional'.)
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

notes.title: Chapter 8 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 8 you should be able to: appreciate the diversity of linguistic meaning; understand that meaning is more than literal word/sentence meaning; see why meaning matters in daily life; use conversational principles to calculate how implicatures are produced; and appreciate neurodiversity in pragmatics (people can compute implicatures differently).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 7
notes.body: ★ SEMANTICS = study of linguistic meaning. LINGUISTIC vs. NON-linguistic meaning ('swill' vs. 'clouds mean rain'). ★ SENSE (concept in the mind) vs. DENOTATION ⟦x⟧ (what it points to in the world; a set for predicates). ★ COMPOSITIONALITY = meaning from PARTS + how COMBINED; idioms are the non-compositional exception. ★ ENTAILMENT (p true ⇒ q true; contradiction test) vs. PRESUPPOSITION (entailment taken for granted) vs. IMPLICATURE (suggested, CANCELLABLE). ★ Lexical meaning ≠ just NECESSARY & SUFFICIENT conditions — categories are FUZZY (prototypes; 'cup or bowl'). ★ COUNT vs. MASS nouns; INDIVIDUAL-level (stable) vs. STAGE-level (temporary) predicates; gradable adjectives = DEGREES on a scale. ★ Dictionary is NOT the authority on meaning. ★ NPIs (any/ever) need negative/downward-entailing contexts.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: 7.12-7.13 Set theory & negative polarity items
notes.body: Denotations can be modelled with basic set theory (membership, subset, intersection), which helps state semantic relations precisely. Negative polarity items (NPIs) like 'any', 'ever', 'lift a finger' are licensed only in negative or otherwise downward-entailing environments ('I didn't see anyone' ✓ vs. *'I saw anyone').
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: 7.10-7.11 Dictionaries & denotation
notes.body: The dictionary is NOT the ultimate authority on meaning: a word used by a community is real even if it's not in the OED, and dictionaries don't list every sense. Formally, denotation is what an expression points to in our cognitive model of the world, written ⟦x⟧. A one-place predicate denotes a set: ⟦sour⟧ = the set of all sour things; ⟦pencil⟧ = the set of all pencils. Sense and denotation are linked — the sense lets you compute the denotation.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: 7.7-7.9 Countability, predicate types, degrees
notes.body: Nouns are used as count (countable, pluralizable, 'many': cats) or mass (uncountable substance, 'much': water) — many nouns can be both. Predicates are individual-level (stable property: is tall) or stage-level (temporary: is available); some Spanish adjectives are ambivalent. Gradable adjectives involve degrees on a scale (tall→taller), and languages differ in how they mark comparison (some, like Washo, lack overt comparative morphemes).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: 7.6 Events & thematic roles
notes.body: Verb meanings can be analysed with event semantics: a sentence asserts there is an event e of a certain type with participants filling thematic roles (agent, theme, experiencer, etc., from Chapter 6). E.g., 'The sound frightened the child' ≈ there is an event e, e is a frightening, the sound is the cause/stimulus, the child is the experiencer.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: 7.4-7.5 The lexicon & lexical meaning
notes.body: A lexical entry pairs a form with syntactic category and semantic (lexical) meaning. One classical theory: word meaning = necessary and sufficient conditions (e.g., 'doe' = [animal, deer, female, adult]). But the 'cup or bowl' experiments show category boundaries are fuzzy — whether something counts as a cup depends on context (e.g., having tea in it) and world knowledge, so meaning involves prototypes, not just strict definitions. Compositional vs. non-compositional (idiomatic) meaning also matters (prebake = compositional; 'let the cat out of the bag' = non-compositional).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: 7.3 Entailments, presuppositions, implicatures
notes.body: When p is true, if q must also be true, p entails q (an entailment). Test with contradiction: if negating q while asserting p is contradictory, it's an entailment. A presupposition is a special entailment the sentence takes for granted ('...again' presupposes a prior event). An implicature is merely suggested, not necessarily true, and is cancellable (negating it isn't a contradiction). So when a sentence 'means' something, ask: entailment, presupposition, or implicature?
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: 7.2 Compositionality
notes.body: The principle of compositionality: the meaning of a complex expression is built from the meanings of its parts AND how they're combined. This holds for sentences (from word meanings + syntactic structure) and for multimorphemic words (unhelpfulness from un-, help, -ful, -ness in a particular structure). It predicts that structural ambiguity yields multiple meanings, and it's why we don't have to memorize whole sentences — only morphemes. Exceptions are idioms, which are non-compositional and stored whole.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: 7.1 Linguistic meaning
notes.body: Semantics is the study of linguistic meaning — how word meanings combine into sentence meaning. Distinguish linguistic meaning (the sense of an expression, e.g., 'what does swill mean?') from non-linguistic meaning ('those clouds mean rain'; a gift 'means' I'm sorry). Use–mention matters: 'strawberry has 4 syllables' talks about the word. Two complementary views of meaning: sense (the concept stored in the mind) and denotation (what the expression points to in the world). Saying ode'imin and strawberry 'mean the same' = they denote the same thing.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: Chapter 7 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 7 you should be able to: acknowledge the plurality of theories about the lexicon; explain why the dictionary isn't the authority on meaning; analyse linguistic meaning from descriptive observations; understand what concepts lexical meaning encodes; and explain the difference between sense and denotation.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 6
notes.body: ★ WORD ORDER fixed (English SVO) vs. flexible (topic/focus). Basic order = S/O/V order; SOV most common, SVO next; all six attested. ★ CLAUSE = subject + predicate; SENTENCE = standalone clause. TRANSITIVITY/valency: intransitive(1)/transitive(2)/ditransitive(3). Sentence types: declarative/interrogative(yes-no, content)/imperative; simple/compound/complex(=embedding=RECURSION). ★ CONSTITUENT = unit; tests = SUBSTITUTION, MOVEMENT, IT-CLEFT, STAND-ALONE, (coordination). ★ HEAD (obligatory core, fixes category) + COMPLEMENT (selected) + SPECIFIER (top edge) + ADJUNCT (modifier). SELECTION = head's complement requirement. ★ LEXICAL (N V Adj Adv) vs. FUNCTIONAL (D, T/Aux, C, pronoun, conj) categories. ★ THEMATIC ROLES: AGENT (on purpose), EXPERIENCER (mental state), THEME/PATIENT (affected), INSTRUMENT. ARGUMENT STRUCTURE changed by PASSIVE. ★ X-BAR: XP → (specifier) X'; X' → X (complement); every phrase projects a HEAD. SENTENCE = TP (subject = spec-TP, T = tense/aux); embedded clause = CP (head C). ★ MOVEMENT: Subj-Aux Inversion = T-to-C HEAD MOVEMENT (yes-no Qs); content Qs = WH-MOVEMENT to spec-CP.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.19-6.20 Movement
notes.body: Transformations relate structures by movement. Subject-Auxiliary Inversion is Head Movement — the auxiliary moves from T into the next-higher head C (T-to-C movement), deriving yes-no questions. Content questions add wh-movement, moving the wh-phrase to the specifier of CP. Movement is notated by striking through the element in its base position and drawing an arrow to its landing site (trace notation, using t, is an alternative not used in this book).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.15-6.18 TP, adjuncts, CP & ambiguity
notes.body: A sentence is a TP (tense phrase): T heads it (an auxiliary, tense on the verb, or nonfinite 'to'), the subject sits in the specifier of TP, and the VP is the complement (sometimes labelled IP/InflP). Modifiers attach as adjuncts — extra bar levels that are neither specifier nor complement. Embedded clauses are CPs headed by a complementizer. Because one string can have two tree structures, syntax produces structural ambiguity (e.g., 'The raccoon thought about the food in that trashcan'), with each structure giving a different meaning.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.13-6.14 Phrase structure & X-bar theory
notes.body: Phrase structure rules (e.g., S → NP VP; NP → (D) (AdjP) N (PP)) generate trees, but don't explain why only certain structures occur. X-bar theory adds constraints: every phrase XP is the projection of a head X through an intermediate bar level X', with fixed slots for a specifier, complement(s), and adjuncts. Crucially, every phrase is headed by a word of the same category (endocentricity), and all categories — including functional ones — project the same X-bar schema.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.10-6.11 Arguments & thematic roles
notes.body: Arguments also carry thematic (theta) roles — the part a participant plays in the event: agent (acts on purpose: 'The pirate sank the ship'), experiencer (has a mental state: 'Pirates frighten me'), theme (the thing something happens to; a patient is additionally changed), instrument (tool: 'with a cannon'), plus goal, source, and causer. A predicate's argument structure is the arguments it needs and the roles it assigns. Operations like the passive change argument structure — the theme becomes the subject and the agent is demoted or optional — without changing the underlying event roles.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.7-6.9 Questions
notes.body: English yes-no questions are formed by Subject-Auxiliary Inversion — swapping the subject and the auxiliary (You have left → Have you left?). Content questions use a wh-word (who/what/where/why/how) and front it. In embedded questions the wh-word still moves, but the main-clause inversion doesn't apply the same way. In X-bar terms (6.19-6.20) these are movement: inversion = T-to-C head movement; wh-questions = wh-movement to the front of the clause (specifier of CP).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.6 Clausal embedding
notes.body: Embedding places one clause inside another: the outer clause is the matrix (main) clause, the inner one the embedded (subordinate) clause, typically introduced by a complementizer (e.g., 'Seo-yeon knows [that Danai laughed]'). Because a clause can contain a clause that contains a clause…, embedding is recursive, giving language its unbounded productivity.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.5 Functional categories
notes.body: Beyond lexical categories (N, V, Adj, Adv), words like the, will, in, that belong to functional categories — the grammatical glue of syntax, often with purely grammatical meaning. Key ones: determiners (D: the, a, this, my, 's — in complementary distribution with one another), auxiliaries (analyzed as T, carrying tense), complementizers (C: that, if, whether), pronouns, and conjunctions/coordinators. Functional categories are closed classes.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.4 Constituency tests
notes.body: Constituency tests show that a string is a single unit. Substitution/pro-form: replace the string with a pronoun/pro-form. Movement: move the string as a block. It-cleft: put the string in 'It is/was ___ that ___' (VPs cleft with 'do'). Stand-alone (fragment): the string can be a one-phrase answer to a question. Coordination: constituents of the same type can be joined by and/or/but (introduced but flagged as less reliable). A test result applies only to the specific sentence tested — 'constituent' is always relative to a structure.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.3 Phrases, heads, and selection
notes.body: Languages group words into constituents; grammar refers to phrases in structural positions, not linear counts. A phrase is a set of words acting as a unit (whatever can replace 'all kittens' as the subject). Every phrase has a head — its obligatory central word, which fixes the phrase's category (a noun heads an NP, a verb a VP). Heads select (require) complements — e.g., a transitive verb selects an object NP; adjectives typically take PP complements. Headedness and constituency are the two central ideas of syntax.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.2 Sentence types & typology
notes.body: By function: declarative (statement), interrogative (question — yes-no or content), imperative (command). By structure: simple (one clause), compound (clauses joined by a coordinator and/or/but), complex (contains an embedded subordinate clause — an example of recursion). Across languages, basic word order is stated as the order of Subject, Object, Verb; SVO and SOV dominate, but all six orders occur, and many languages allow far more flexibility than English.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.2 Key grammatical terminology
notes.body: A sentence expresses a complete statement/question/command; a statement expresses a proposition (true or false). A clause = a subject + a predicate (the state/event attributed to the subject). Arguments are phrases (usually NPs) for the event's participants. Subjects precede the predicate in English and control agreement (nominative pronouns: I, we, they); direct objects follow the verb (accusative: me, us, them); indirect objects (ditransitives) are often the recipient, often marked by 'to'. Transitivity (valency) = number of arguments: intransitive (1), transitive (2), ditransitive (3).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: 6.1-6.2 Syntactic knowledge & word order
notes.body: Syntax is knowledge of how words combine into phrases and sentences; speakers judge some orders grammatical and others not. Word order can be fixed (English, French) or flexible (Latin, Kanien'kéha, ASL — where order tracks topic/focus). English requires the verb to follow the subject: schematically N V (N). Basic word order describes subject/object/verb order in neutral declaratives: English is SVO (~35% of languages); SOV is most common worldwide (~41%); VSO and object-initial orders also exist. Flexible-order languages are often topic-comment (first element = topic, rest = comment).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: Chapter 6 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 6 you should be able to: use constituency tests to identify the phrases in a sentence; categorize words into lexical and functional categories by distribution; identify relationships between grammatically related sentences (active/passive, statements/questions); and draw tree diagrams representing the structure of English sentences.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 5
notes.body: ★ MORPHEME = smallest form + meaning/function pairing. WORD = smallest SEPARABLE unit (not the spelling definition). Complex = >1 morpheme. ★ ROOT (indivisible core) vs. BASE (what an affix attaches to) vs. AFFIX (bound). Affix types: PREFIX, SUFFIX, CIRCUMFIX, INFIX, SIMULTANEOUS. FREE (stands alone) vs. BOUND (must attach; only roots can be free). ★ BEYOND AFFIXES: internal change (mouse→mice), suppletion (go→went, memorized), reduplication (salad-salad). ★ TYPOLOGY: isolating/analytic vs. synthetic → agglutinative (separable, one-meaning) vs. fusional (one affix = many meanings). ★ ALLOMORPHY: allomorphs = variant forms; PHONOLOGICALLY conditioned (a/an; plural [s]/[z]/[ɪz]) vs. LEXICALLY conditioned (ox→oxen). ZERO affix = ∅. ★ LEXICAL CATEGORY defined by DISTRIBUTION, not meaning. ★ DERIVATION changes meaning/CATEGORY (new word); INFLECTION expresses grammatical info and NEVER changes category. ★ COMPOUND = 2+ ROOTS; English stress on FIRST member. ★ STRUCTURAL AMBIGUITY = one string, two structures/meanings (unlockable); shown with morphological TREES.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.9-5.11 Structure, trees & solving problems
notes.body: Words have internal structure, which can create structural ambiguity: one string with two possible structures and meanings (e.g., unlockable = 'able to be unlocked' [[un-lock]-able] vs. 'unable to be locked' [un-[lock-able]]). We show structure with morphological tree diagrams built by successive affixation. To solve an unfamiliar-language morphology problem, compare glossed forms, line up recurring form-meaning pairings, and isolate each morpheme's form, meaning, and position.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.8 Compounding
notes.body: Compounding builds a word from two or more roots (blackboard, dog-tired, dishwasher). English compounds freely across categories (N-N, Adj-N, V-N, etc.). Spelling is inconsistent (solid, hyphenated, or spaced), so it's an unreliable test; a better cue is stress — English compounds are stressed on the FIRST member (gréenhouse vs. green hóuse). Compounding differs from derivation and inflection because it combines roots rather than adding affixes.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.7 Inflectional morphology
notes.body: Inflectional morphology expresses grammatical information appropriate to a word's category and NEVER changes the category. English has a small inflectional system: noun plural -s and possessive -'s; verb 3rd-person-singular present -s, past -ed, and participles; adjective comparative -er / superlative -est. Other languages inflect far more (case, gender, agreement, tense/aspect/mood). Some 'inflectional' meanings can instead be shown syntactically (e.g., 'will' for future) — that's not inflectional morphology.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.6 Derivational morphology
notes.body: Derivational morphology changes the meaning and/or the lexical category of its base, building a new word: teach (V) + -er → teacher (N); happy (Adj) + -ness → happiness (N); un- + kind → unkind (meaning change, same category). Derivation is often not fully productive (idiosyncratic, with gaps) and typically sits closer to the root than inflection. It's how languages expand the lexicon.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.5 Lexical categories
notes.body: A lexical category (part of speech) is a group of words that behave the same for grammatical purposes. Crucially, linguists define categories by DISTRIBUTION (the grammatical contexts a word appears in), not by meaning — semantic tests ('a noun is a person/place/thing') fail on cases like action and event (both nouns). Tests for the four lexical categories (noun, verb, adjective, adverb) mix syntactic distribution (e.g., nouns follow determiners, can be subjects/objects, take plurals) and morphological behaviour. Morphology divides into derivational and inflectional, plus compounding.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.4 Allomorphy
notes.body: Allomorphy is when one morpheme (consistent meaning) has different forms (allomorphs) by environment.
